# Summary {.unnumbered}

We provide estimates of the carbon sequestration ecosystem service for the 27 Member States of the European Union in 2000, 2006,
2012, 2018 and 2024, following the accounting method of @vallecillo2019 and its update in @lanotte2021. In 2024, land removes
{{< fact removals_mt_2024 >}} million tonnes of CO2 and emits {{< fact emissions_mt_2024 >}} million tonnes. The actual flow that
reaches society after this offset is {{< fact flow_mt_2024 >}} million tonnes, against {{< fact flow_mt_2000 >}} million tonnes in
2000, and it is worth {{< fact value_constant_bn_2024 >}} billion euro at constant 2010 prices. The missed flow, which is the part of
the removals used up by those emissions, is worth {{< fact missed_constant_bn_2024 >}} billion euro. The value rests on a social
cost of carbon of EUR 343.6 per tonne of carbon, which is EUR {{< fact price_2023 >}} per tonne of CO2, in 2023 euros.

# Introduction

Carbon sequestration is the uptake of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere by ecosystems, mainly through the growth of trees,
which stores carbon in biomass and soil. Ecosystem accounting treats it as a contribution to global climate regulation that benefits
society as a whole. Ecosystems also release CO2, so the accounts need to separate what land removes from what land emits, and to
establish how much of the removals is left once those emissions are compensated [@lanotte2021].

This report describes how we estimated those quantities and valued them, why we took each decision along the way and what the
estimates show. The terms in @tbl-terms recur throughout the report.

| Term | Meaning in this report |
|:---|:-----|
| LULUCF | Land use, land use change and forestry, the part of the greenhouse gas inventory that reports the CO2 exchanged between land and the atmosphere. |
| Removal | CO2 taken up by a land category in a country and year, when the category is a net sink. |
| Emission | CO2 released by a land category in a country and year, when the category is a net source. |
| Offset | The netting of all emissions of land against all removals, at the level of the European Union. |
| Actual flow | The net CO2 that ecosystems deliver to society after the offset. |
| Flow without offset | The total removals of the land categories, before their emissions are subtracted. |
| Missed flow | The flow without offset minus the actual flow, which is the part of the removals that compensates the emissions of land use. |
| GDMP | Gross Dry Matter Productivity, the rate at which vegetation produces dry matter, estimated from satellite images. |
| NUTS | The European classification of territorial units, where NUTS0 is the country level. |

: Key terms of the report. {#tbl-terms}

# Results

## Removals, emissions and actual flow

Forest land provides {{< fact forest_share_of_removals_2024 >}} percent of the removals in 2024 (@tbl-categories). The balance of
forest land moves from {{< fact balance_CRF4A_2012 >}} million tonnes in 2012 to {{< fact balance_CRF4A_2018 >}} million tonnes in
2018 and {{< fact balance_CRF4A_2024 >}} million tonnes in 2024, and it drives the series (@fig-series). The actual flow is
{{< fact flow_mt_2012 >}} million tonnes in 2012, {{< fact flow_mt_2018 >}} million tonnes in 2018 and {{< fact flow_mt_2024 >}}
million tonnes in 2024 (@tbl-eu). Values of recent years may change with new releases of the inventory.

::: {#tbl-categories}
{{< datatable balance_by_category >}}

Signed balance by category in the EU27, in million tonnes of CO2, with uptake as positive. The codes CRF4G and CRF4H stay outside the flow.
:::

::: {#tbl-eu}
{{< datatable eu_series >}}

Removals, emissions, actual flow and missed flow in the EU27, in million tonnes of CO2.
:::

## Countries

Under @eq-flow, the actual flow of a country follows its forest removals, so the flow is concentrated. Five countries hold
{{< fact top5_share >}} percent of the actual flow in 2024, led by {{< fact top5_countries >}} (@tbl-countries and @fig-countries).
@tbl-country-counts counts, in each reporting year, the countries without forest removals, which have no actual flow in that year,
and the countries whose land as a whole emits more than it removes.

::: {#tbl-countries}
{{< datatable flow_by_country >}}

Accounts by country in 2024, in thousand tonnes of CO2.
:::

## Regions

The workbook holds every quantity at NUTS0, NUTS2 and NUTS3. @tbl-regions lists the NUTS2 regions with the largest actual flow in
2024, which are the large forest regions of the countries with the highest removals.

::: {#tbl-regions}

NUTS2 regions with the largest actual flow in 2024, in thousand tonnes of CO2, with the value in million euro at constant 2010 prices.
:::

## Maps

@fig-flow-maps shows the actual flow, drawn at 10 km from the 1 km working layers so that it reads at this size. Forest regions of high productivity stand out
within each country, and the differences between countries reflect their national values, so borders can show as steps in the map.
@vallecillo2019 note the same effect. Countries with no forest removals in a year appear blank in that panel. Productivity only places
values within a country, so it has no effect on national totals (@tbl-forest-area). The value maps in @fig-value-maps follow the same
pattern, since they multiply the flow by one price per year.

::: {#tbl-forest-area}
{{< datatable forest_area >}}

Forest on the 1 km grid and in the regional tables, and mean productivity on cells that are mostly forest, by reporting year.
:::

![Actual flow at 10 km, in thousand tonnes of CO2 per cell, on a square root scale.](figures/carbon_flow_maps.png){#fig-flow-maps width=100%}

![Value of the actual flow at 10 km, in million euro at constant 2010 prices per cell, on a square root scale.](figures/carbon_value_maps.png){#fig-value-maps width=100%}

## Value

The actual flow is worth {{< fact value_constant_bn_2024 >}} billion euro in 2024 at constant 2010 prices, and
{{< fact value_current_bn_2024 >}} billion euro in current prices (@tbl-value and @fig-value). Constant values follow the physical
flow, because the real price is fixed. The price per tonne of each reporting year is in @tbl-price.

::: {#tbl-value}
{{< datatable value_eu_series >}}

Value in the EU27, in million euro.
:::

::: {#tbl-price}
{{< datatable carbon_price >}}

Social cost of carbon per tonne of CO2, in 2023 euros and in the euros of each year.
:::

![Value of the actual flow and of the missed flow in the EU27, at constant 2010 prices.](figures/carbon_value_series.png){#fig-value width=100%}

## Sectors

@tbl-sectors shows the actual flow attributed to the sectors that emit CO2. The largest part in 2024 goes to
{{< fact top_sector >}}, with {{< fact top_sector_mt >}} million tonnes. The attribution follows the emissions of each country weighted
by its flow, so it also shifts when the flow moves between countries.

::: {#tbl-sectors}
{{< datatable sector_by_year >}}

Actual flow attributed to emitting sectors in the EU27, in million tonnes of CO2.
:::

## Comparison with the published accounts

@lanotte2021 report an actual flow of 306 million tonnes of CO2 in 2012 in their main tables, from forest removals of 444 million
tonnes. We obtain {{< fact flow_mt_2012 >}} million tonnes (@tbl-published). The comparison serves for orientation only, because they
report the EU-28 with an earlier release of the inventory, and countries revise past years in each release. The price also differs by
design. Their flow of 2012 is valued at 9,189 million euro, which implies EUR {{< fact price_published_2012 >}} per tonne, whereas the
price here in 2012 is EUR {{< fact price_implied_2012 >}} per tonne in current prices.

::: {#tbl-published}
{{< datatable published_flow >}}

Actual flow in this report (EU27) and in La Notte et al. (2021), Table 6.7 (EU-28), in million tonnes of CO2.
:::

# Limitations

**Inventories.** Countries produce their inventories with their own methods and definitions, so comparisons between countries call
for caution [@vallecillo2019]. They revise them every year, which changes the values of past years between releases. Some sharp
changes between years may reflect these methods as well as forests, and we did not separate the two.

**Actual flow.** The flow of a country depends on the removals and emissions of all countries, because the offset is computed once
for the European Union, and it should not be read as a national balance. The tables show that balance separately. A category counts
as a removal or an emission according to its net sign in each country and year, so the gross fluxes inside a category are not
visible. Countries with no forest removals in a year receive no flow, so their value can change abruptly between years when their
forest moves between source and sink. Harvested wood products stay outside the flow, and including them as a deduction would lower
the removals of forest land by up to the sink in @tbl-comparison.

**Maps.** The spatial key combines where forest is located with the productivity of the vegetation, which is a proxy for where
removals happen. Productivity measures growth and does not measure the net carbon balance, so it does not capture the carbon in soils
or the age of stands. The maps of 2000, 2006 and 2012 use a 1 km product and those of 2018 and 2024 a 300 m product, so the spatial
detail of the two groups differs. The Corine accounting layers have a minimum mapping unit of 25 hectares. Maps and regional values
allocate a national value, so they should not be read as independent local estimates. The regional tables use the 1 km key and the
maps the 100 m key, so a sum of the 100 m maps over a region can differ slightly from its value in the tables. The map of the flow without the offset covers
forest land only.

**Value.** The value depends directly on the price. The social cost of carbon is a model-based estimate that is sensitive to
assumptions such as the discount rate and the damage function. This literature quotes estimates per tonne of carbon and per tonne of
CO2, which differ by a factor of 44/12, and the value adopted here is per tonne of carbon, the unit in which the meta-analysis
standardises its estimates. The real price is several times the benchmark of earlier accounts, so the values cannot be compared with
those accounts. It also differs from a market price. A consumer price index for the whole European Union converts values to constant
prices, so differences in inflation between countries are ignored.
